summary: Compares two proposals for supporting IPv6 in the DNS, the A6 approach and the AAAA approach, and examines the pros and cons of each. It was written to clarify a debate that had not reached consensus, so the IETF could reach closure. It updates RFCs 2673 and 2874.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3364 compares two kinds of DNS record for storing IPv6 addresses. It explains when storing an address in pieces could help and why a complete-address record is simpler to look up.

questions: what are the tradeoffs for ipv6 dns support
what is a dns bit label
what is the difference between aaaa and a6 records
subtitle: A 2002 comparison of AAAA and A6 records for storing IPv6 addresses in DNS.

tldr.problem: The IETF had two proposed ways to support IPv6 addresses in DNS and had not reached agreement on which approach to use.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3364 compares the simpler AAAA record with A6 records that can represent an address in fragments, including effects on lookup, updates, DNSSEC and reverse mapping.
tldr.outcome: The note recommends A6 and DNAME only if rapid renumbering or GSE-like routing is intended; otherwise it recommends AAAA. In either case it favors textual labels for reverse mapping over bit labels.

facts.label: A6 lookup approach
facts.value: Can fetch an address in fragments

facts.label: Reverse-tree recommendation
facts.value: Use textual labels rather than bit labels

today: RFC 3364 is an Informational note that updates RFC 2673 and RFC 2874. It compares proposals and gives conditional recommendations; it does not specify a new standard.

sections.title: Two Ways to Store an IPv6 Address
sections.content:
RFC 1886 defines the AAAA record, which stores a complete IPv6 address in one DNS record. RFC 2874 defines A6 records, which can split an address into fragments and link those fragments through prefix names. Both proposals were listed as Proposed Standards when this note was written.

The note asks whether the added flexibility of A6 is needed and weighs its operational costs against AAAA. It is an analysis and recommendation, not a new DNS standard.
sections.plainLanguage: One record type stores a complete IPv6 address in one place. The other can store it in linked pieces, which may simplify some updates but takes more work to look up.

sections.title: Where Each Record Has an Advantage
sections.content:
A6 can change part of an address without updating the zone that stores the remaining part. The RFC says this may help with rapid renumbering or routing designs that change address prefixes. AAAA is more familiar from the IPv4 A-record model and is optimized for reading: a resolver gets a complete address instead of fetching its pieces separately.

The trade-off is that A6 can reduce work when address data is written, while AAAA can reduce work when data is read. The RFC notes that A6 with a zero-length prefix has the same meaning as AAAA.
sections.plainLanguage: Storing address pieces can make some changes easier. Storing the whole address in one record lets DNS software retrieve it in one step.

sections.title: Lookup Cost, DNSSEC and Transition
sections.content:
Resolving a chain of A6 records can require several queries, so a longer chain may take longer and may fail if one part cannot be resolved. The note warns against indiscriminate use of long chains. It also explains that DNSSEC signing may require less work after some renumbering with A6, while validating fragments can require more signatures and larger responses.

A resolver could synthesize an AAAA answer from A6 queries during a transition, but the synthesized answer cannot carry an equivalent DNSSEC signature. Clients that validate DNSSEC themselves would need to query A6 directly in that case.
sections.plainLanguage: Each address piece can add another lookup step, and each signed piece adds security-checking work. DNS software can build a complete-address answer from fragments, but cannot attach the same kind of DNSSEC proof.

sections.title: Reverse Mapping and the Final Choice
sections.content:
For reverse mapping, the note compares textual hexadecimal labels with a proposed DNS bit-label type. Bit labels are more compact, but they would require authoritative servers and resolvers to understand a new label type. The RFC concludes that the textual form is adequate. It links the case for DNAME records in the reverse tree to the case for fragmented A6 records in the main tree.

The recommendation depends on whether the IPv6 community intends rapid renumbering or GSE-like routing. If so, the note recommends A6 and DNAME as needed. If not, it recommends keeping AAAA and not using DNAME; either way it recommends textual reverse-tree labels.
sections.plainLanguage: The note recommends the simpler AAAA approach unless IPv6 needs address fragments for rapid renumbering or similar routing. For reverse lookups, it recommends the textual format because existing DNS software can process it.
